title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a conch at dusk and a drum in the street: two ways of loving God in one country

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram, and its last story here: Tirumular, who entered a cowherd's body for the sake of grieving cows, and said love itself is Shiva. Did you let someone's distress move you? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

Dusk in a Bengali village. In one courtyard, someone lifts a conch shell and blows it, a long round note, and lights a lamp before a small image of the Goddess. A few lanes over, a clay drum starts up, a cymbal joins it, and a handful of people begin singing the names of Krishna, louder and faster, until a couple of them are swaying with their arms in the air. Same village, same evening, two sounds. Today we cross the subcontinent to Bengal, and meet two streams of devotion that run through it side by side.
screen: `A CONCH AT DUSK.` → `A DRUM IN THE NEXT LANE.` → `TWO STREAMS, ONE VILLAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the conch and the lamp. The Shakta stream worships God as the Goddess, as Shakti, the power that makes and moves everything. In Bengal she has many faces: Durga riding her lion, Kali dark and fierce. And the name devotees call her is the simplest one there is: Ma. Mother. A text the Shaktas treasure, the Devi Mahatmya, tells of the Goddess rising up when the gods themselves can't defeat the demons, and saying, in paraphrase, that whenever trouble comes, she will come again. Now the drum. The Vaishnava stream worships Vishnu, and in Bengal, above all, Krishna, the cowherd of Vrindavan, and Radha, who loves him. Tradition says this stream was set alight by Chaitanya, a teacher from Nabadwip, who led people through the streets singing the names of God together. That singing is called kirtan, and it's still the heart of it: the name, sung out loud, in company. Turn it once. These two can sound like opposites: a fierce Mother with a sword, a flute-playing boy in a meadow. But they share a grammar. Both call God by a close family name, Mother on one side, and on the other, beloved, child, friend. Both lean on singing more than on argument. Turn it again. These are streams, not walls. Later this week we'll meet a priest of Kali who also wept for Krishna, and singers whose songs borrow from more than one stream. Over the next days we'll follow each stream in turn, and watch where they meet.
screen: `SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER` · `KRISHNA, SUNG IN THE STREETS` · `TWO STREAMS, ONE GRAMMAR` · `STREAMS, NOT WALLS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two sounds. Sit, and let the breath slow. First, one long sound: hum quietly on an out-breath, low and round, like the conch. Let it fade into silence. Then, for a few breaths, let the breath be quicker and lighter, like a drum starting up, then let it settle again. Notice which one your body likes today: the long note or the quick one. If you pray, you can let one name for God ride on the out-breath, Ma, or Krishna, or the name you use. The bell holds the time.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Two ways of devotion running side by side: the Goddess called Mother, and Krishna sung in the street. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, listen for two sounds that share your street or your home, and notice how they live side by side. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: In Bengal, Shakta devotees worship the Goddess as Durga and Kali, at home and at autumn festivals, while Vaishnava devotees gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna together to drum and cymbals.
